lead: A reverse-biased Zener diode enters controlled breakdown at a set voltage, then holds almost that same voltage across itself even when its current changes. That makes it a cheap voltage reference. Put a resistor in series and a Zener across the load, and a rough 12 V adapter can feed a steady 6 V circuit. You find this inside small chargers and sensor boards. Older regulator ICs used a Zener as the voltage reference; the 78xx family and the LM317 use a bandgap reference instead.
prereq: You need 4.1: the reverse characteristic of a PN junction and what breakdown means.

sections.h3: How a Zener diode holds a voltage

blocks.text: A Zener diode is a PN junction doped much more heavily than an ordinary diode. The heavy doping makes the depletion layer very thin, so even a small reverse voltage creates a large electric field across it. At a designed reverse voltage Vz, the Zener voltage, the field tears electrons out of their bonds and current jumps. This is Zener breakdown, and it happens below about 5 V. Above about 5 V the same sudden current comes from avalanche breakdown: carriers gain enough energy to knock more carriers loose. Both are reversible if the current is limited, and both hold the voltage nearly constant.

Useful ratings: Vz is the nominal voltage at a test current; Iz(min) is the knee current below which regulation fails; Iz(max) is the largest current the package can take; Zz = ΔVz/ΔIz is the dynamic resistance, a few ohms to tens of ohms in breakdown. Power dissipated is Pz = Vz × Iz. A 6 V Zener passing 68 mA burns 0.41 W, so it needs a 1 W part, not a 0.5 W part. Below about 5 V, Vz falls as temperature rises; above about 5 V, Vz rises slightly with temperature.

blocks.where: Pz is the Zener power in watts, Vz is the Zener voltage in volts, and Iz is the Zener current in amperes.

blocks.text: The Zener sits in parallel with the load, and a series resistor Rs drops the difference between the unregulated input Vin and Vz. Kirchhoff's current law at the output node gives I_Rs = Iz + IL, where IL is the load current. The resistor must be small enough to keep Iz above Iz(min) at the lowest Vin and the largest IL, yet large enough to keep Iz below Iz(max) at the highest Vin and the smallest IL.

items: Find the largest allowed Rs from the worst low-input, high-load case: Rs(max) = (Vin(min) − Vz)/(Iz(min) + IL(max)).
Find the smallest allowed Rs from the worst high-input, low-load case: Rs(min) = (Vin(max) − Vz)/(Iz(max) + IL(min)).
Choose a standard resistor value between Rs(min) and Rs(max).
Check Iz at both extremes, then compute the worst-case Zener power Pz = Vz × Iz(worst), where Iz(worst) is the largest actual Zener current found, at Vin(max) and IL(min).

blocks.where: Rs is the series resistor in ohms, Vin is the unregulated input in volts, Vz is the Zener voltage in volts, Iz is the Zener current in amperes, and IL is the load current in amperes.

blocks.text: line regulation = ΔVout / ΔVin;   load regulation = (V_no-load − V_full-load) / V_full-load × 100%
blocks.where: ΔVout is the change in output voltage for a change ΔVin in input voltage; V_no-load and V_full-load are the output voltages at no load and full load. Line regulation is often quoted in mV/V, load regulation in percent.

blocks.text: A three-terminal regulator hides a voltage reference, an error amplifier and a pass transistor inside one package. The 78xx family gives a fixed positive output: 7805 is 5 V, 7812 is 12 V. The 79xx family gives the same fixed values but negative output. The input must stay above the output by the dropout voltage, about 2 V for the classic 78xx and less for low-dropout types. Input and output capacitors keep the chip stable and improve ripple rejection, the ratio of input ripple to output ripple, often 60 dB to 70 dB for a 78xx.

The LM317 is adjustable. It holds 1.25 V between its OUT and ADJ pins, so R1 from OUT to ADJ carries a fixed current and R2 from ADJ to ground sets the output. Vout = 1.25(1 + R2/R1). With R1 = 240 Ω and R2 = 1 kΩ, Vout = 1.25(1 + 1000/240) = 6.46 V. Keep a minimum load of a few milliamperes. The LM317 also needs about 2 V dropout, so a 6 V output needs at least about 8 V at the input.

blocks.where: Vout is the regulated output in volts, R1 is the resistor from OUT to ADJ in ohms, and R2 is the resistor from ADJ to ground in ohms; 1.25 V is the internal reference.

figure.caption: The 12 V supply drops across Rs and the 6 V Zener; the Zener current plus the 20–50 mA load current flows through Rs. Notice the Zener is reverse biased and sits in parallel with the load.

spec.title: Shunt Zener regulator
spec.aria: Block diagram: unregulated 12 V passes through series resistor Rs to the output node, where a reverse-biased 6 V Zener and the load sit in parallel.

examples.question: A 6 V Zener must feed a load current varying from 20 mA to 50 mA from an unregulated 12 V supply that can sag to 10 V. Take Iz(min) = 5 mA and Iz(max) = 100 mA. Choose Rs and the Zener power rating. Use a standard resistor if it lies inside the allowed range.
steps: Data: Vz = 6 V; Vin(min) = 10 V; Vin(max) = 12 V; IL(min) = 20 mA; IL(max) = 50 mA; Iz(min) = 5 mA; Iz(max) = 100 mA.
Largest Rs: at Vin = 10 V and IL = 50 mA, I_Rs must be at least 5 mA + 50 mA = 55 mA. Rs(max) = (10 − 6) V / 0.055 A = 4 / 0.055 = 72.7 Ω.
Smallest Rs: at Vin = 12 V and IL = 20 mA, I_Rs must not exceed 100 mA + 20 mA = 120 mA. Rs(min) = (12 − 6) V / 0.120 A = 6 / 0.120 = 50 Ω.
Choose the standard 68 Ω, which lies between 50 Ω and 72.7 Ω.
Low-input check: at 10 V and full load, I_Rs = (10 − 6) / 68 = 58.82 mA. Iz = 58.82 − 50 = 8.82 mA, above 5 mA.
High-input check: at 12 V and light load, I_Rs = (12 − 6) / 68 = 88.24 mA. Iz = 88.24 − 20 = 68.24 mA, below 100 mA.
Worst Zener power: Pz = 6 V × 0.06824 A = 0.409 W. A 0.5 W part is too close, so fit a 1 W Zener.
examples.answer: Rs = 68 Ω, inside the allowed 50 Ω to 72.7 Ω range; worst-case Zener dissipation is 0.41 W, so use a 1 W Zener.
examples.check:
Vz = 6.0
Vin_min = 10.0
Vin_max = 12.0
IL_min = 0.020
IL_max = 0.050
Iz_min = 0.005
Iz_max = 0.100
Rs_max = (Vin_min - Vz) / (Iz_min + IL_max)
Rs_min = (Vin_max - Vz) / (Iz_max + IL_min)
Rs = 68.0
Iz_low_input = (Vin_min - Vz) / Rs - IL_max
Iz_high_input = (Vin_max - Vz) / Rs - IL_min
Pz = Vz * Iz_high_input
print(round(Rs_max, 3))
print(round(Rs_min, 3))
print(round(Iz_low_input * 1000, 3))
print(round(Iz_high_input * 1000, 3))
print(round(Pz, 4))

traps: Sizing Rs from the no-load case only. Then at full load Iz falls below Iz(min) and the output sags.
Assuming regulation continues when Vin < Vz, or when Iz < Iz(min). The output then just follows the input, reduced by the divider.
Using Pz = Vz × Iz(test) instead of the worst case at maximum Vin and minimum load, where the Zener burns the most power.
Swapping the families: 78xx is positive, 79xx is negative. The LM317 reference is 1.25 V between OUT and ADJ, not 0 V.
Forgetting dropout voltage. A 7805 needs roughly 7 V or more at its input to hold 5 V; below that the output falls.

quiz.q: What does the label 7805 on a three-terminal regulator mean?
quiz.a: It is a fixed positive 5 V regulator: the 78 family is positive, and 05 gives 5 V.

quiz.q: Why does a Zener diode hold a nearly constant voltage when its reverse current changes?
quiz.a: In breakdown, a large change in current causes only a small change in voltage because the dynamic resistance Zz is small. The heavy doping gives a thin depletion layer and a steep reverse characteristic.

quiz.q: State one difference between Zener breakdown and avalanche breakdown.
quiz.a: Zener breakdown occurs below about 5 V by tunnelling in a very thin depletion layer; avalanche breakdown occurs above about 5 V by impact ionisation. Both are reversible when the current is limited.

quiz.q: A 5.1 V Zener is fed from a 9 V supply. The load current varies from 10 mA to 30 mA. Take Iz(min) = 5 mA and Iz(max) = 60 mA. Find the allowed range of Rs and choose a standard value.
In the worked 68 Ω, 6 V circuit, Vin falls to 5 V. What happens to the output?
quiz.a: Vin is below Vz, so the Zener is off. The output is Vin × RL/(Rs + RL). With RL between 120 Ω and 300 Ω, the output is about 3.2 V to 4.1 V, not 6 V. Regulation is lost.

quiz.q: Why is the Zener power worst at maximum input voltage and minimum load current?
quiz.a: The series resistor current is largest at high Vin, and the load takes least current at light load, so the excess current flows through the Zener. Pz = Vz × Iz is then maximum.

quiz.q: An LM317 has R1 = 240 Ω from OUT to ADJ and R2 = 1 kΩ from ADJ to ground. Find Vout.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern boards mostly use low-dropout linear regulators and switching converters; the Zener survives as a clamp, a reference and a cheap shunt regulator. At chip level, bandgap references use the predictable temperature behaviour of bipolar transistors to make 1.25 V or 2.5 V references. Search “LM317 datasheet”, “LDO dropout voltage” and “TL431 shunt reference” to go further.
